notes: Original developed narrative and full practice retained. Open slots: mano, appuntamento and parola. Unstressed object clitics, demonstratives, embedded questions, new past tense and audio remain absent.

Uscire was introduced receptively at chapter 9; this chapter promotes production at its planned date and adds the actual infinitive. Preserve first-reading date 9 and sense identity; introduce its first productive card now.

Lexical homograph correction: noun il lavoro already occurs in chapter 7 (including its English grammar examples), whereas io lavoro was the earlier verb. Record noun first reading at 7, explicit production at planned chapter 10, and add the correct noun popup alongside the verb. Earlier prose and plan rows are untouched.

Actual appointment is today after four, after Marco’s public hours; the public reading meeting stays tomorrow at three. Letter returns sealed to Ada; she authorizes coming with the damaged chair. The chapter plans the return, and the repair remains for chapter 11.

Delivered hours/work, capacity, material, desire/arrival, hand, generic blue-chair repair, work/free-time and appointment aids accompany first-use stages. The repair illustration is a meaning example, not a claim that Ada’s white chair is repaired. Current infinitive uscire is translated accurately while its published reading sense ID remains intact; lexicon-copy warning is the person-versus-infinitive gloss difference, not a new meaning. Low gloss density should be assessed against these delivered aids and actual prose, not waived.

segments.text: Elena guarda la porta della bottega. Un foglio ha un titolo: «Orario di apertura». Sotto sono due parole, oggi e domani. L’orario è dalle ore due alle ore quattro. La riunione è domani alle tre: dentro l’orario di apertura. Marco è al tavolo; Elena ha la busta chiusa e la foto. Paolo legge il foglio sulla porta.

La gamba è di legno; l’attrezzo è di ferro. Sul tavolo sono pezzi di legno e un attrezzo di ferro. Marco guarda ancora la gamba rotta.

segments.text: «Voi potete portare la sedia? Voi volete aiutare Marco?»

grammar.title: Grammatica
grammar.rule: posso / devo / voglio + venire; possiamo / dobbiamo / vogliamo + portare.
grammar.note_en:
The three modal verbs express ability or permission, obligation, and desire. Posso means “I can/may”; devo means “I must/have to”; voglio means “I want”. They normally introduce an infinitive, the verb’s dictionary form: posso venire, “I can come”; devo lavorare, “I have to work”; voglio aiutare, “I want to help”. The modal changes to match its subject, while the infinitive stays the same: io posso venire, voi potete venire. Here it is the modal that carries person and number. The table gives the present forms actually demonstrated in the story.

Potere has posso/puoi/può/possiamo/potete/possono: “I can, you can, can, we can, you can, they can”. Its meaning depends on context. Posso dare una mano? offers help by asking whether the speaker can help. Potete venire grants permission or confirms the arrangement. Marco non può uscire explains a constraint: he must work during opening hours. Do not turn can into one universal permission rule; ability and circumstances matter too. The accent belongs in può.

Dovere has devo/devi/deve/dobbiamo/dovete/devono: “I must, you must, must, we must, you must, they must”. It can express an obligation, a necessary step or an agreed responsibility. Marco deve lavorare states his work obligation; dobbiamo portare la sedia states the step needed for its repair. Volere has voglio/vuoi/vuole/vogliamo/volete/vogliono: “I want, you want, wants, we want, you want, they want”. Voglio venire expresses Marco’s desire; it does not prove he is able to come during the meeting. Wanting and being able are deliberately contrasted.

The infinitive endings -are/-ere/-ire are visible in forms already connected to familiar actions: portare (“carry/bring”), leggere (“read”), venire (“come”). These words are not commands. In the demonstrated modal-plus-infinitive pattern, no a or di goes between the modal and the infinitive: posso venire, devo portare, voglio parlare. Fare means “do/make”: fare un lavoro, “do a job”. Dare means “give”; dare una mano literally means “give a hand” and idiomatically means “lend a hand/help”. Stare means “stay/remain”: devo stare in bottega, “I must stay in the workshop”. Uscire means “go out/leave”; earlier esce/escono are present forms of this same verb, now given explicit productive teaching.

Lavoro as a noun means “work/job”, while io lavoro is a verb meaning “I work”. Legno is wood as a material; ferro is iron. La gamba è di legno means “the leg is made of wood”. The construction avere bisogno di means “need”: ho bisogno di tempo, “I need time”; abbiamo bisogno di Ada, “we need Ada”. Di can join an article here too: ho bisogno della mia sedia, “I need my chair”. Tempo libero is “free time”, contrasted here with the scheduled work. An appuntamento is an agreed appointment/meeting, distinct from the public riunione (“meeting/gathering”) planned for tomorrow.

The opening-hours notice uses dalle due alle quattro, “from two until four”. Dalle joins da + le; alle joins a + le. In alle tre, “at three”, the feminine plural article belongs to the clock-time expression; it does not agree with the person arriving. Dopo le quattro means “after four”. These time expressions apply the prepositions already learned. Ad Ada, “to Ada”, uses the variant ad especially before another a. The appointment is today after closing; the public meeting is tomorrow during Marco’s opening hours. A present modal can describe that arranged future responsibility without a new future-tense paradigm.

Translations of the displayed models: Marco non può uscire means “Marco cannot go out/leave”; Marco vuole parlare con Ada means “Marco wants to talk to Ada”; Noi dobbiamo andare in biblioteca means “We have to go to the library”; Voi potete portare la sedia? means “Can you, plural, bring the chair?” Posso dare una mano? means “Can I lend a hand?”; potete venire means “you, plural, can/may come”. Marco deve lavorare means “Marco must work”; dobbiamo portare la sedia means “we have to bring the chair”; voglio venire means “I want to come”; devo portare means “I have to carry/bring”; voglio parlare means “I want to speak/talk”. Io posso venire / voi potete venire mean “I can come / you, plural, can come”. Esce/escono mean “he or she goes out / they go out”.

The short rule combines posso/devo/voglio venire, “I can/have to/want to come”, and possiamo/dobbiamo/vogliamo portare, “we can/have to/want to carry/bring”. In the clock table, da is “from”, a is “at” here, and le is the feminine plural “the”; these parts join in dalle and alle.
